newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Malan awaits fate as S.African judge reads verdict.
newsitem.headline: Malan awaits fate as S.African judge reads verdict.

text.p: Former South African defence minister Magnus Malan, the most senior figure charged with atrocities against blacks, returned to court on Thursday to hear the verdict in his seven-month trial for murder.

Malan and 15 co-defendants face 13 counts of murder for a death squad attack on the family of a black activist nine years ago. The case is South Africa's biggest trial to date of apartheid-era human rights abuses.

The defendants sat in the supreme court in the Indian Ocean port of Durban, near the township scene of the massacre, as Judge Jan Hugo began to read what was expected to be a lengthy verdict, possibly taking up to two days.
Malan is the highest member of the old apartheid government to be charged with abuses committed to maintain white minority rule over the black majority.
He and his co-accused have repeatedly declared their innocence during the trial.
Malan, head of the armed forces before he entered the cabinet, admits he helped set up a paramilitary force for Inkatha, the main black rivals of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress.
But he says the force was legitimate and that if it had any hand in the massacre of seven adults and six young children, he knew nothing about it.

The verdict is eagerly awaited by supporters of the old regime who have called the trial a witch hunt, and by opponents who say the masters, not just their lackeys who did the dirty work, must pay for the crimes of apartheid.
Co-defendants include six Zulu police accused of carrying out the attack, a top Inkatha official, three generals, two majors, a vice-admiral, a brigadier and a senior policeman.
Four of the original 20 accused were acquitted earlier because of a lack of evidence against them.
